title: How the maps were made - Ancient vegetation reconstruction
meta: Czyżewski et al. 2026, Giesecke et al. 2017, Pearce et al. 2023

body.html: The maps in this atlas app are not photographs of the past. They are reconstructions: nine time slices of Northwestern Europe, from the Last Glacial Maximum (c. 25,500 BCE) to the Atlantic period (c. 4,500 BCE). Each map is built from interpreted geological and ecological evidence and then rendered to look like a satellite image.

This essay documents how the maps were created: which basemaps were used, what data was used to model ancient vegetation trends, and which assumptions and interpretations were made. We value transparency, so that you can judge the ancient landscape map reconstructions for yourself.

body.html: The starting point is a set of schematic, polygon-based palaeogeographic reconstructions developed for the European Prehistoric Heritage Atlas project (EPHA). Such grey polygon-based maps are useful for specialists but hard to read for everyone else.

The aim of the Ancient Europe atlas is to translate the schematic maps into scientifically defensible ancient landscape maps, combining scientific datasets on vegetation and fauna trends with the basemaps and translating that into ancient vegetation reconstruction maps for the same nine geological periods.

Vegetation cover in each zone is described by a three-way percentage split: open woodland, fully open ground and closed canopy. The Central zone is the anchor for the European-average canopy-structure estimate of the period, drawn from Czyżewski et al. (2026) and adjusted regionally using Giesecke et al. (2017) and Kern et al. (2025). Because this rests on European-average estimates and a limited number of regional sources rather than a site-resolved pollen synthesis for every zone, the table carries a medium confidence rating overall.

Two climatic regimes are distinguished. In a mild regime, with the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) active, the share of closed canopy decreases from Coastal to Central to Northern: the warmer, oceanically buffered coast is more wooded than the cooler north. In a hard regime — AMOC shutdown, or a coast pressed against an ice margin — this ordering inverts, because the Coastal zone lies against the ice and becomes sparser than the Central zone. Two periods are treated as hard regimes: the Last Glacial Maximum and the Younger Dryas, the latter being the less extreme of the two. In both, the Coastal zone is treated as internally heterogeneous. Instead of a single mix it is rendered with an internal sigmoid gradient, called “Option A”, driven by distance to the ice-sheet polygon. The gradient runs from a barren ice-margin endpoint to a more wooded refugium endpoint representing the southern Coastal extent, such as the Atlantic coast of northern Spain.

body.note: In the two hard-regime periods the Coastal zone is not given a single mix. It is rendered as a gradient from an ice-margin endpoint (first triple) to a more wooded refugium endpoint (second triple).

body.html: Figure 2 shows how these modelled results translate to natural landscape colours on the maps. The legend translates the closed-canopy share into six vegetation-structure classes, each with its own colour, from open steppe and tundra (under 5%) to closed-canopy forest (over 55%). Applied to Table 1, the Central zone during the LGM (4% closed canopy) falls in the open steppe and tundra class. The Coastal zone in the Early Boreal (28%) is woodland with open patches, the Northern zone in the Atlantic period (40%) is mixed deciduous forest, and the Atlantic Coastal zone (75%) is closed-canopy forest. These are zone-level values: within a zone, the noise texture and the sigmoid blends mean that the colour you see varies around them.

body.text: Ancient vegetation trends and how megafauna controlled openness versus canopy closure

body.html: The modelled percentages are not arbitrary; they are derived from ancient vegetation datasets and interpretation of what kept European landscapes open or let them close from Czyżewski et al. (2026) and adjusted regionally using Giesecke et al. (2017) and Kern et al. (2025).

As the European continent warmed after the end of the last Ice Age, we see that the tree-species arrival follows the classic pollen-zone sequence: birch and pine pioneers, then hazel, then the thermophilous deciduous trees, and then elm, oak, lime, alder and ash.

The drivers of openness versus canopy closure, however, change markedly through the sequence in line with megafauna trends. In the early part of the record, from the LGM to the Allerød, openness was maintained mainly by large herbivores rather than by climate or fire alone. This is the logic of the mammoth-steppe model, supported by sedimentary ancient-DNA evidence in which forbs dominate over grasses. Czyżewski et al. (2026) synthesise this evidence into the argument that a woodland–grassland mosaic, not a closed forest, was Europe’s prevailing natural state.

As megafauna populations collapsed through the Holocene, that regulating mechanism was progressively lost. From the Early Preboreal onwards, fire — increasingly of human origin — and the surviving smaller herbivores (red deer, roe deer, wild boar and, locally, aurochs) took over as the main landscape structuring agents. This also matters for the natural forest baseline interpretations. The closed-canopy forest of the Atlantic period looks like the climax of the series, but reconstructions of the Last Interglacial (Eemian), when megaherbivores were still present, point to a far more open structure: roughly 60% open woodland, 19% fully open ground and 22% closed canopy (Pearce et al. 2023). The Atlantic forest is therefore best read as a post-megafauna landscape — closed not because it represents an unmodified natural state, but because the animals that had kept interglacial woodland open were already gone.
The individual period vegetation (flora) and fauna trends are described in the app’s Flora & Fauna panels.

body.text: About the workflow: from GIS polygons to classmasks

body.html: The workflow combines the GIS source basemap data with newly interpreted classmasks, digital elevation models, and drainage networks, with a procedural Python rendering pipeline that turns schematic vegetation and hydrology classes into textured, georeferenced raster output.

Every time slice begins as an EPHA base map: a GeoTIFF classmask in EPSG:3035 (the European equal-area projection) with seven integer classes. Class 1 is sea or ocean, class 2 the ice sheet, class 3 ice lake and class 4 lake. Classes 5, 6 and 7 are three vegetation sub-zones: Northern, Central and Coastal. The masks were originally digitised as interpreted polygons (land area, ice sheet, ice lake, lake) and then reclassified into this seven-class scheme.

The three vegetation zones are deliberately coarse. They capture the dominant climatic gradient across the map area — from the oceanically buffered coast, through a Central belt that serves as the proxy for the European average, to a cooler, more continental north — without pretending to resolve every regional pollen record. The Atlantic period served as the pilot for the pipeline because its coastline closely approximates today's, which allows the present-day elevation model to be used directly. The method was then extended to the eight earlier periods, with bathymetric data added wherever sea level and coastline differed substantially from the present.
Each classmask passes through the same sequence of steps.

Relief. A 1000 m resolution digital elevation model is shaded with a relief-adaptive hillshade. Above a relief threshold (in the range 0.40–0.80) a distinct rocky-highland tint is applied, so that mountain terrain separates visibly from lowland.

Vegetation texture. Each vegetation zone is filled with organic, multi-scale noise. The noise is modulated by the period-specific canopy-percentage mix described above, so that a woodland-rich period looks different from an open steppe not just in colour but in grain.

Blending. Transitions between neighbouring vegetation zones are rendered as smooth sigmoid blends driven by spatial distance transforms, rather than as hard polygon edges. Real vegetation boundaries are gradients, and the same technique is reused inside a single zone where the evidence calls for it (see “Option A” above).

Hydrology. Palaeo-rivers and valleys are extracted from the EPHA drainage-systems shapefile, filtered to the “river valley” and “palaeo valley” feature types, reprojected to EPSG:3035 and skeletonised. The result is a continuous, vector-derived river network appropriate to each period.
Output. Each period is exported as an RGBA PNG with transparent no-data regions and as a georeferenced GeoTIFF, which feeds the MapLibre and PMTiles web-tile pipeline used by the app.
A reconstruction is only as useful as its stated limits. Four are known and documented.

Regional resolution. The three-zone scheme does not resolve secondary regional effects: an early forest refugium on the Iberian Atlantic coast, delayed postglacial recolonisation in Norway, and forest-steppe dynamics in the east, in Ukraine. These are candidates for a more granular zonation in a later version.

Confidence. The canopy-percentage table rests on European-average estimates regionally adjusted with a limited set of sources, and is rated medium confidence overall. The maps should be read as well-reasoned structural reconstructions at regional level, not as site-resolved vegetation surveys.

Black Sea. For the periods before it reconnected with the Mediterranean (the Littorina transgression, c. 7,850 BCE), the Black Sea was a freshwater basin and should be classified as a lake rather than as sea. This correction has been identified but not yet applied.
Baltic Ice Lake. The Younger Dryas render reuses the Early Boreal lake footprint as a geometric proxy. This is a documented simplification, not an independent reconstruction of the lake.
